traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Benin court art from c. 13th c. CE

traditions.geographic_origin: Upper Nile, South Sudan and western Ethiopia

traditions.earliest_attestation: Kingdom of Kongo, 14th c. CE; Portuguese records from 1480s
traditions.geographic_origin: Lower Congo River: DR Congo, Republic of Congo, Angola

traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Great Zimbabwe period c. 11th–15th c. CE

traditions.name: Khoikhoi / Khoekhoe
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded from 17th c. CE

traditions.name: Serer (Senegal / Gambia)
traditions.geographic_origin: Sine-Saloum region, Senegal and the Gambia

traditions.geographic_origin: Northern shore of Lake Victoria, Uganda

traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded from 17th c. CE

traditions.earliest_attestation: Libyan Ammon cult by 6th c. BCE; Roman-era Libyan gods; living folk rites
traditions.geographic_origin: North Africa from Siwa oasis to the Atlantic

traditions.earliest_attestation: early 20th c. CE (Rio de Janeiro, c. 1908 traditional founding)

Espiritismo (Puerto Rico / Cuba)

traditions.geographic_origin: Rio Grande and Acoma–Laguna region, New Mexico

traditions.name: Maidu (California)
traditions.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded early 20th c. CE

iconography: iron staff topped with a bird
deities.summary: Lord of leaves and of every healing plant. No medicine works, no rite is complete, without his herbs; the saying goes "kosi ewe, kosi orisa" — without leaves there is no orisha. He is one-legged, one-eyed, and speaks in a high voice through his bird.
The divine hunter and tracker, whose arrow never misses its mark. He is the orisha of the forest, of pursuit and of justice, and companion of Ogun and Eshu among the warrior orisha.

iconography: layered cloth masquerade costume covering the whole body
deities.summary: The collective ancestors returning to the living in masquerade. When the Egungun dance in their layered cloth, the dead of the lineage walk in the town again, bless their descendants and enforce the moral order.
Owner of the deep ocean, beyond Yemoja's shallows. Olokun holds the unfathomed depths, their wealth and their terror; once Olokun rose to flood the earth and was chained at the sea's bottom.

iconography: pair of carved ere ibeji figures
deities.summary: The divine twins, born as Taiwo (the first to taste the world) and Kehinde (the one who came behind and is the elder). Twins carry great power; when a twin dies an ere ibeji figure is carved and cared for as the living child.
Orisha of the farm, the harvest and the fertile earth. He judges disputes among the orisha and guards against witchcraft; the yam harvest is his.

Progenitor of the Yoruba kings, who descended from heaven at Ile-Ife with a chain, a handful of earth and a five-toed hen and made dry land where there was only water. All crowned Yoruba kings trace their lineage to his sons.

iconography: ibori (beaded cowrie shrine of the head)
deities.summary: The divine head: each person's personal destiny-deity, chosen in heaven before birth. Ifá teaches that no orisha can bless a person without the consent of their Ori; Ori alone follows a person all the way to the end.
Death personified, one of the ajogun (warrior-forces against humanity). Iku comes when the days written in a person's Ori run out, and Orunmila's sacrifices can turn him away before his time.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; royal Dahomey cult 17th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Lord of the earth and of smallpox. Sakpata punishes with disease those who wrong the earth and heals those who honor him; the kings of Dahomey feared his priests and at times banished his cult.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; royal Dahomey cult 17th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: The thunder vodun, head of the sky pantheon. His thunderbolt strikes liars and thieves; the ram and the double axe are his.

iconography: human figure with a blade for a head
deities.summary: Vodun of iron, war and tools; the sword Mawu-Lisa used to shape the world. Gu was sent to earth to clear the bush and teach humans to work metal.

The cosmic serpent, coiled under and around the earth, who carried Mawu-Lisa in his mouth as the world was made and holds it together. The rainbow is his body; motion, wealth and life-force flow through him.
Master of the sea, chief of the water vodun (Hu), who sends rain and the fish.
The divine voice of destiny read through divination. Fa is the "word of Mawu", each person's fate written before birth and disclosed by the bokonon (diviner).
The great abosom (god) of the Tano River, war and thunder, eldest son of Nyame among the river gods. He is invoked by Asante and Bono for strength in battle.
Eldest son of Nyame, god of the Bia River and of the bush, who lost his inheritance of the fertile lands to his younger brother Tano by trickery.
The hook-footed monster of the deep forest, who dangles his legs from the high branches to snatch travelers; ally of witches (abayifo).
The trickster-spirit of war, chaos and bargains, who drives warriors to fury and is called on for victory. Igbo tradition knows him as a dangerous but necessary force, not an absolute evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; carved figures from 19th c. CE
iconography: horned seated figure holding a knife and a tusk or head
deities.summary: The horned personal god of the right hand: a man's strength, will and achievement. A man consecrates his Ikenga and offers to it before an undertaking, and it is split and buried with him at death.
The spirit of divination, healing and creative madness. Agwu calls the dibia (diviner-healer) to his work, and those he chooses but who refuse him are troubled until they accept.
The sun, eye of Chukwu, giver of light, knowledge and perfection; Igbo prayers turn to the rising sun.
The personal guardian spirit and destiny given to each person by Chukwu. "Onye kwe, chi ya ekwe" — when a person says yes, his chi says yes too.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: The supreme creator of the Edo, who sent his sons to found the world; the youngest took a snail shell of earth and so became owner of the land.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: Son of Osanobua and king of the waters, source of wealth, children and beauty. Women keep his white altars; the Oba of Benin is his earthly counterpart.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: The king of death, who rules the dead and claims the blood offered to him.

deities.etymology: Shared with Maasai Enkai/Ngai; commonly taken as a loan from Maa.
deities.summary: The one creator and giver of all things, who lives in the sky and comes to rest on Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya). People pray facing the mountain; he is approached through elders and sacrifice under the sacred mugumo fig tree.
The first man and woman, placed by Ngai at Mukurwe wa Nyagathanga; their nine daughters became the mothers of the nine Kikuyu clans.

alternate_names: Nhialic (Divinity, the one in the sky)
deities.summary: Divinity, the creator in the sky. Once heaven was close and joined to earth by a rope, until the first woman struck it with her hoe; Nhialic withdrew, and death and toil entered the world.
The great free-divinity of rain, lightning and fertility, the most powerful of the powers between Nhialic and people.
The first woman, patron of women and gardens, whose hoe struck the sky and caused Divinity to withdraw. Her emblem is the little snake.
The first man, a free-divinity associated with the sun, fire and illness.
Spirit, the creator who is like wind and air, everywhere present yet in the sky. He is the father of all, who gives and takes life, and to whom the Nuer submit in all misfortune.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Portuguese records from 16th c. CE
primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
deities.summary: The supreme creator, Nzambi the all-powerful, who made the world and stands above all spirits; he is not given shrines but is the source of all power the minkisi carry.

primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
iconography: mirror-sealed medicine pack in the belly
deities.summary: Spirit-powers held in consecrated containers and carved figures. Each nkisi is a spirit from the land of the dead bound into an object by the nganga (ritual expert); the nkondi, studded with nails, hunts down oath-breakers and witches.

primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
iconography: the Kongo cosmogram (dikenga) with its horizontal line
deities.summary: The great water that divides the land of the living from the land of the dead. The sun crosses it daily; the soul crosses it at death and is reborn on the far side; the Kongo cosmogram marks it as the horizontal line.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Capuchin records 17th c. CE
primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
deities.summary: Spirits of water and stone, bound to particular springs, pools and rocks, who protect the land and its people and can make places fertile or dangerous.
The red, cruel first king, identified with the rainbow serpent, who ruled without manners or law until he was overthrown by his nephew Kalala Ilunga.
The refined hunter-prince from the east who brought good manners and sacred kingship; father of Kalala Ilunga by Nkongolo's sister.
Hero-son of Mbidi Kiluwe, who defeated Nkongolo and founded the second Luba empire and its sacred kingship.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Matopo shrine cult from at least 17th c. CE
deities.summary: The high God of rain and fertility, who speaks as a voice from the caves of the Matopo Hills. Mwari is both male and female, sky and pool, and is approached through the oracle and through the mhondoro spirits.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; spirit medium attested 1890s CE
deities.summary: A great mhondoro (royal ancestral lion-spirit) who speaks through female mediums. Through the medium Charwe she led resistance in the 1896–97 rising and prophesied, "my bones will rise again."

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; medium attested 19th c. CE
deities.summary: A powerful mhondoro and prophet-spirit, guardian of the Shona, remembered for prophesying the coming of foreigners.

The first-appearing one, God of the sky, thunder and earthquakes, who existed before all things. Where uNkulunkulu is the first ancestor who brought people out of the reeds, uMvelinqangi is the one who was first of all.
The Princess of Heaven, daughter of God, maiden of rain, rainbow and the growing crops. In spring girls honor her with songs and gardens so she will bless the harvest.
The ancestral spirits of the lineage, who watch over their descendants, speak through dreams and the izangoma diviners, and are fed with beer and cattle.
A small, malicious water-sprite sent by witches to cause illness and harm, against which people raise their beds on bricks.

The supreme creator of the Xhosa. When he made the world the sea-dragon tried to destroy it, and his mother Djobela, the earth, raised the four giants to hold the world's corners as mountains. He is invoked with a stone thrown on the cairn.
deities.tradition_claim: Later Xhosa Christianity used uThixo, a word drawn from the Khoikhoi divine name, for God.

alternate_names: Gauwa (as high god, in some reports)
deities.summary: The great god of the Ju|'hoan, who made the earth, the animals and people and lives in the eastern sky. In the old stories he was a trickster who behaved outrageously; now he is the giver of life and death.
The lesser god of the west and the spirits of the dead (ǁgauwasi), who shoots invisible arrows of sickness and death and plays tricks on people; in the healing dance the healers fight him off.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.etymology: Often rendered "wounded knee"; later Xhosa uThixo is widely traced to this name.
deities.summary: The rain-giver and great chief of the Khoikhoi, who lives in the red sky of dawn, sends the thunderclouds and fought ǁGaunab, the lord of the dark sky. He was killed and rose again, stronger with each wound.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The lord of darkness, death and the black sky, enemy of Tsui-ǁGoab, who brings sickness and lives among the dead in the west.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The great hunter, magician and culture hero, born of a cow that ate grass, who died many times and rose again; his many graves are the stone cairns where travelers add a stone for luck.
The oldest ancestor, who died and was reborn as a serpent; he carries the life-force of the earth and the growth of the fields, and his priest the Hogon is fed by him at night.
The androgynous spirit of the river Niger, of water, speech and order, who reorganized the world after Pemba's disorder, gave the seasons and taught people speech and law.

The first creative being, who came from the primal vibration as a seed and made the earth, then sought to dominate creation through his acacia tree and the women he made; his rule brought disorder until Faro intervened.
The first woman, Pemba's companion, who rebelled and ran through the world spreading impurity, sorcery and disorder, yet also brought agriculture.
The supreme deity of the Serer, both near and far, male and female, to whom the saltigue (seer-priests) turn in the yearly Xooy divination for the rains.
The ancestral and saintly spirits, often in serpent form, who mediate between Roog and the living and are honored at shrines and sacred trees.
The creator and father of the gods, who made all things and stands above the lubaale (national gods).
Benevolent lubaale of Lake Victoria, giver of fish, children, health and plenty; his chief shrine was on the Ssese Islands.
The war god of Buganda, brother of Mukasa, who fought for the kingdom from the clouds and was mortally wounded by a captive woman who learned his secret.
Death, brother of Nambi, who followed her and Kintu to earth when she turned back for millet; ever since he kills people and hides in the earth.
The first man and first king of Buganda, who passed the tests of Gulu, the sky-king, to win his daughter Nambi.

primary_sources: Oromo oral tradition and women's Ateetee ritual
deities.summary: The Oromo goddess of fertility and motherhood, honored by women with songs and offerings to bring childbirth and protect families.

The creator, the "Fragrant Lord" in the sky. In one tale the god of the sky and the god of the earth both made people — the earth-god shaped the bodies and the sky-god gave the breath — so at death the body returns to earth and the breath to heaven.
The ancestors, closest powers to the living, honored in the famadihana (turning of the bones), when the dead are rewrapped in new shrouds and danced with.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 3rd c. BCE (Musawwarat es-Sufra Lion Temple)
primary_sources: Lion Temple inscriptions at Musawwarat es-Sufra (hymn to Apedemak)
iconography: lion head on a man's body
lion-headed serpent rising from a lotus
deities.summary: The lion-headed war god of Meroë, "Lion of the South, strong of arm," who goes before the king in battle and grants victory, abundance and the king's rule. At Naqa he appears as a lion-headed serpent rising from a lotus.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 15th c. BCE (Egyptian temple); Kushite royal cult from 8th c. BCE
iconography: Jebel Barkal pinnacle (seen as a uraeus)
deities.summary: Amun who dwells in the Pure Mountain of Jebel Barkal and chooses the kings of Kush. By his oracle the Napatan kings were crowned, and Piye marched north in his name to conquer Egypt.

primary_sources: Musawwarat es-Sufra temple statues and inscriptions
deities.summary: Meroitic god of procreation and creation, guardian of temple doorways together with Arensnuphis.

primary_sources: Musawwarat es-Sufra and Philae temple inscriptions
deities.summary: Kushite god, "the good companion," hunter and guardian, later honored at Philae alongside Egyptian gods and equated with Shu and Onuris.
The ram-horned god of the oracle in the Siwa oasis, known throughout the Libyan desert and the Greek world. Alexander crossed the sand to consult him and was hailed as his son.
The bull-horned war god of the Laguatan Libyans, born of Ammon and a cow, whose image was carried into battle before the warriors.

primary_sources: Amazigh folk ritual of Taslit n Unzar (Bride of Anzar)
deities.summary: The rain god of Amazigh folk tradition, who loved a maiden and withheld the rain until she gave herself to him; in drought villages carry a doll, the Bride of Anzar, in procession to bring the rain.

Virgin martyr shut in a tower by her pagan father, who beheaded her for her faith and was struck dead by lightning. She is patron of artillerymen, miners and all in danger of sudden death, and is invoked against thunder and fire.

The poor man covered with sores who lay at the rich man's gate, whose wounds the dogs licked, and who was carried by angels to Abraham's bosom. Popular devotion venerates him as patron of the sick, lepers and the poor.

deities.earliest_attestation: Cuban shrine from 17th c. CE (Spanish devotion from 5th c. legend)
deities.summary: The Black Virgin of Regla, patroness of Havana harbor and of sailors, whose image crossed the sea and is honored in the bay of Havana.
Prince of the Apostles, the rock on which Christ built his Church, to whom Christ gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven; he guards the gates of heaven.
Soldier-martyr of Lydda who slew the dragon to free a captive princess and a city; patron of soldiers and knights.
Franciscan preacher and miracle-worker, finder of lost things, patron of the poor and of travelers, who held the Christ Child in a vision.

deities.earliest_attestation: Spanish devotion 13th c. legend; Mexican shrine (Plateros) 19th c. CE
primary_sources: Shrine tradition of Atocha (Madrid) and Plateros (Fresnillo, Zacatecas)
iconography: child in pilgrim's cape and plumed hat
deities.summary: The Christ Child dressed as a pilgrim, with basket, staff and gourd, who in the legend brought food and water to Christian prisoners when no adult could. He wanders at night helping travelers, prisoners and the trapped, wearing out his shoes.

deities.earliest_attestation: icon venerated from 14th c. CE (Jasna Góra)
iconography: two parallel scars on the right cheek
deities.summary: The Black Madonna icon of Jasna Góra, Queen and Protector of Poland, whose cheek bears two scars from a sword cut; she defended the monastery in the siege of 1655.

deities.primary_name: Our Lady of Charity of El Cobre
alternate_names: Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre
iconography: Virgin in gold on the waves
deities.summary: The image of the Virgin found floating on the Bay of Nipe by three men in a boat — two Indigenous brothers and an enslaved African boy — in a storm. She is patroness of Cuba, honored at El Cobre near the copper mines.
The Virgin in white who inspired the founding of the Mercedarian order to ransom Christian captives; patroness of captives and prisoners.

primary_sources: Fray Alonso de Espinosa, Del origen y milagros de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria (1594)
deities.summary: The Virgin of Candlemas, bearing a candle, whose image appeared to the Guanches of Tenerife; patroness of the Canary Islands.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1st c. CE; warrior apparition legend 9th c. (Clavijo)
iconography: knight on a white horse with sword
deities.summary: Apostle, son of thunder, first apostle martyred; in Spain he appears on a white horse leading Christian armies and is patron of soldiers and pilgrims.
The forerunner who baptized Christ in the Jordan, voice crying in the wilderness, beheaded by Herod.
Apostle of Ireland who, according to legend, drove the snakes out of the island and taught the Trinity with the shamrock.
Pious farm laborer of Madrid whose plowing angels finished while he prayed; patron of farmers and harvests.

iconography: young man bound to a tree pierced by arrows
deities.summary: Roman soldier-martyr shot with arrows, who survived and was later beaten to death; patron of soldiers, archers and protector against plague; patron of Rio de Janeiro.
The Virgin of the Seven Sorrows, her heart pierced by swords, adorned and grieving at the foot of the Cross.

primary_sources: Thomas of Celano, Lives of Saint Francis
deities.summary: Founder of the Franciscans, lover of poverty and creation, who received the stigmata.
Twin physicians who healed without payment and were martyred together; patrons of doctors and of children.

deities.primary_name: Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception
deities.summary: The Virgin conceived without original sin, crowned with stars and standing on the moon and the serpent.

deities.etymology: Haitian Creole, from French "Bon Dieu" (Good God).
deities.summary: The Good God, Gran Mèt, creator of all and the one true God, who is far above human affairs. Bondye does not intervene directly; the lwa serve as his intermediaries, and every ceremony begins with prayers to him.

The family of lwa of death, sex and laughter, the spirits of the dead who are honored at Fèt Gede (All Souls). They wear black and purple, speak nasally, joke obscenely and heal children; no one dies unless the Gede dig the grave.

iconography: white woman in purple and black
deities.summary: Wife of Baron Samedi and mother of the Gede, guardian of graves and cemeteries. The first woman buried in a cemetery belongs to her, and her cross guards the dead.

The divine twins, the first children, honored right after Legba at the start of a ceremony. They are innocence and power together, greedy children who must be fed, and the mystery of the one that is two.

The fierce Petwo mother, protector of women, children and the wronged, with scars on her cheek. She is said to have fought in the Haitian Revolution and lost her tongue; she speaks only "ke-ke-ke." Her love is fierce and her vengeance terrible.
The first oungan, patron of priests, healing and the sacred trees, especially the mapou; he gave the asson (sacred rattle) and the knowledge of leaves.
Master of the crossroads in the Petwo rite, the dark counterpart of Legba, who controls the night roads and lets in or keeps out the dangerous spirits.
The peasant lwa of agriculture and the harvest, country cousin in straw hat and blue denim with his makout bag, shrewd and suspicious of city people.
The rainbow serpent, wife of Damballa; together they encircle the cosmos and hold up the sky.

The aspect of God closest to the world in Lucumí theology: Olodumare is God beyond, Olorun the sun, and Olofi the one who personally governs creation and gave the orishas their powers. He is often identified with Jesus Christ.
The first orisha saluted and the last dismissed, owner of the roads and of every crossroads. A child and an old man at once, he opens and closes all doors; without him no offering reaches any orisha.
Mother of all orishas and of all life, queen of the sea, whose seven skirts are the seven seas. She is the protector of motherhood and the patroness of Havana bay.

Father of the world, orisha of smallpox, leprosy and all contagion, and their healer. He walks on crutches with his dogs, covered in sackcloth, and on December 17 thousands walk to his shrine at El Rincón.
Warrior orisha of iron, the forest and work, who clears the way with his machete; one of the Guerreros received with Elegguá and Ochosi.
Orisha of the river, love, sweetness and gold, youngest and most beloved of the orishas, whose laughter hides her sorrow and whose honey softens all.
Orisha of winds, storms and the gates of the cemetery, warrior wife of Changó, who rules the boundary of life and death.
The messenger and the movement of axé: Exu carries offerings to the orixás and is fed first in the padê so the ceremony can proceed. He is mouth, motion and communication itself.
Orixá of iron, war and roads, the blacksmith who opens paths through the forest.
Orixá of the hunt and the forest, patron of the Ketu nation, the hunter of a single arrow who feeds his people.
Orixá of disease, the earth and healing, covered from head to foot in straw (filá) so no one sees the brilliance or the wounds beneath; the young form is Obaluaiê, the elder Omolu.
Orixá of winds, storms and lightning and leader of the eguns (spirits of the dead), Xangô's warrior wife.
Orixá of thunder, fire and justice, king of Oyo, whose double axe (oxê) strikes the unjust.
The supreme God of Umbanda, creator of all, beyond the reach of ritual; the orixás are his forces and the spirit guides his workers of charity.
The spirits of elderly Africans who suffered slavery in Brazil and became wise, humble healers. They smoke pipes, speak slowly, sit on low stools and counsel the troubled with patience.
The spirits of Indigenous Brazilians, proud and strong, masters of the forest and its herbs, who heal and cleanse with cigars and leaves.

alternate_names: Povo da Rua (people of the street)
deities.summary: In Umbanda the exus are a phalanx of spirits — once human — who work at the crossroads and cemetery as guardians and enforcers, policing the boundary between light and darkness. Disciplined exus serve the good.

deities.etymology: From Kimbundu Bombo Nzila / Pambu Nzila, the spirit of the crossroads.
deities.summary: The female exus: spirits of passionate, independent women of the streets, who laugh, drink and help in matters of love, desire and women's struggles.
A great lord of the crossroads in Quimbanda, "he who locks the streets," who can bar or open every road, guard his devotees and lock the ways of their enemies.

deities.earliest_attestation: 20th c. CE (figure from 14th c. Castilian history)
deities.summary: Queen of the pombagiras in Quimbanda, a spirit of power, seduction and sorcery, said to have lived as the mistress of a Castilian king. She rules love magic, binding and the protection of women.
deities.tradition_claim: Identified in Iberian-Brazilian lore with María de Padilla, mistress of Pedro I of Castile.

deities.summary: The supreme God of Palo, creator of all, who gave the mpungus their power and the dead their place; every Palo ceremony invokes "Sambia arriba, Sambia abajo."
The mpungu of iron, war and work, whose nganga is an iron cauldron full of tools and chains.
The mpungu of thunder and lightning, fire and virility, who strikes with seven bolts.
The morning star and guardian of roads in Palo, who opens and closes the paths and is saluted first.
The mpungu of the cemetery, of winds and of the dead, a fierce female power who commands the spirits.

deities.etymology: Usually traced to Akan divine epithets (cf. Onyankopon, Odomankoma).
deities.summary: The supreme creator of Winti, who made the world and the winti spirits; he is not worshipped directly but stands over the pantheons of sky, earth, water and forest.
The earth mother, head of the earth pantheon, guardian of the land, fertility and morality.
The great snake winti, among the most powerful spirits of the earth pantheon, associated with wisdom, healing and possession.
The sky god and supreme power of Kumina, invoked with drumming and songs alongside the ancestral spirits (bakulu) and earthbound spirits who possess dancers.
Thunder orisha and head of the Trinidad Orisha faith, whose name the whole religion bore; his feasts are held with drumming and possession under the shrine flags.
Warrior orisha of iron and war, honored with the sword and the red flag in Trinidad Orisha shrines.

primary_sources: Allan Kardec, The Spirits' Book (1857) as foundational text
deities.summary: A spirit guide of Puerto Rican and Cuban Espiritismo: the spirit of a wise Afro-Caribbean woman, healer and midwife, who comes in white with her scarf and gives spiritual cleansing and counsel.

primary_sources: Allan Kardec, The Spirits' Book (1857) as foundational text
deities.summary: A spirit guide of Espiritismo: the spirit of an Indigenous warrior or healer who protects the medium and fights off dark spirits.

primary_sources: African American folklore (recorded by the Federal Writers' Project, 1930s)
Zora Neale Hurston, "High John de Conquer" (1943)
deities.summary: An African prince sold into slavery who could never be broken, the trickster-hero who outwitted Old Massa and kept hope and laughter alive. When he went back to Africa he left his power in the root that bears his name, carried for luck, strength and success.

alternate_names: the Black Man at the crossroads
deities.summary: The tall dark man who meets you at the crossroads at midnight after nine nights of practice; he takes your guitar or tools, tunes them and hands them back, and from then on you can play or do anything.

primary_sources: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas (c. 1535)
Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Book 6
deities.summary: The Dual God, Lord and Lady of Duality, who dwells in Omeyocan, the thirteenth heaven. Ometeotl is the self-generating source who brought forth the four Tezcatlipocas and sends the souls of infants down to be born.
deities.tradition_claim: Some Nahua philosophical readings treat Ometeotl as the single dual principle underlying all gods.

primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Book 7
Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, 1558)
iconography: face at the center of the Calendar Stone
deities.summary: The Fifth Sun, born when the humble god Nanahuatzin leapt into the fire at Teotihuacan. He refused to move until the gods gave him their blood; his motion must be sustained by sacrifice, and the warriors who die in battle accompany him to the zenith.

primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Book 7
Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, 1558)
deities.summary: The poor, scab-covered god who threw himself into the divine fire at Teotihuacan when the proud Tecciztecatl hesitated, and rose as the sun.

primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Book 7
deities.summary: The rich and proud god who volunteered to become the sun but four times shrank from the fire; leaping after Nanahuatzin, he became the moon, dimmed by a rabbit thrown in his face.

primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577)
deities.summary: Goddess of love, beauty, flowers, desire and the crafts of women — weaving and embroidery. She dwells in Tamoanchan, the paradise of flowers, and was stolen from Tlaloc by Tezcatlipoca.

iconography: coyote head on a human figure with drum
deities.summary: Old Coyote, god of music, dance, mischief and storytelling, patron of the day Cuetzpalin and a lover of feasts and pranks.

primary_sources: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas (c. 1535)
iconography: squatting figure with clawed limbs and mouths at the joints
deities.summary: The earth monster, a great toad-like being with mouths at every joint, torn in two by Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca to make the earth and sky. Her hair became the trees and her mouths the caves and rivers; she cries at night for the blood of the dead.

primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Book 3 (appendix on burial)
deities.summary: Queen of Mictlan and wife of Mictlantecuhtli, keeper of the bones of the dead.

primary_sources: Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, 1558)
deities.summary: Dog-headed twin of Quetzalcoatl, god of the evening star, monstrosity and twins, who guides the dead through Mictlan and helped bring up the bones of humanity.

deities.earliest_attestation: Postclassic (Old Fire God imagery from Formative period)
primary_sources: Florentine Codex (Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general, c. 1577) Books 1, 7
deities.summary: The Old God of fire and of the year, the Turquoise Lord who sits at the center of the world and the hearth; at the New Fire ceremony every 52 years his fire is drilled anew to save the world.
Goddess of the maguey plant, mother of the four hundred rabbit gods of drunkenness (Centzon Totochtin), who nurses them with pulque from her many breasts.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE (Motul dictionary; Books of Chilam Balam)
deities.summary: The One God, sole living and true god, greatest of all the gods of Yucatán, who has no form and cannot be represented; father of Itzamna.
deities.tradition_claim: Modern New Age writings popularized a "Hunab Ku" symbol; that symbol is an Aztec-derived design and not Maya.

primary_sources: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1550s; Ximénez manuscript c. 1701)
deities.summary: The Sovereign, one of the Framers and Shapers who in the stillness of the primordial sea spoke with Gucumatz and brought forth the earth by the word.

deities.earliest_attestation: written c. 1550s (Popol Vuh); highland cult Postclassic
primary_sources: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1550s; Ximénez manuscript c. 1701)
deities.summary: The Sovereign Plumed Serpent of the K'iche', who with Tepeu and Heart of Sky created the world through speech; later a K'iche' king took his power and became serpent, eagle and jaguar.

primary_sources: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán (c. 1566)
deities.summary: The Feathered Serpent of Yucatán, worshipped at Chichén Itzá and Mayapán, remembered as a lord who came from the west and ruled and gave laws; at the equinox his shadow-serpent descends the pyramid steps.

primary_sources: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1550s; Ximénez manuscript c. 1701)
deities.etymology: K'iche' juraqan, usually "one leg"; resemblance to Taíno huracán (source of English "hurricane") is debated.
deities.summary: Heart of Sky, the one-legged god of storm, lightning and wind, with his lightnings Caculha Huracan, Chipi Caculha and Raxa Caculha. He sent the flood that destroyed the wooden people.

iconography: square eyes, filed front teeth, kin (sun) sign
deities.summary: The Sun-Faced Lord, the sun god, whose title K'inich was taken by kings; at night he travels through the underworld as the Jaguar Sun.

primary_sources: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán (c. 1566)
deities.summary: The rope-woman who receives those who die by hanging and carries them to paradise, together with warriors, priests and women who die in childbirth.
deities.tradition_claim: The iconography often linked to her (a hanging woman in the Dresden Codex) is not named in the codex.

deities.earliest_attestation: written c. 1550s (Popol Vuh); Late Preclassic imagery (Izapa)
primary_sources: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1550s; Ximénez manuscript c. 1701)
deities.summary: Seven Macaw, the false sun who boasted in the age before the true sun that he was the sun and moon, glittering with metal eyes and jeweled teeth, until the Hero Twins shot him down and removed his splendor.
The lord of death and the earthquake who rules the underworld beneath the earth, where he punishes souls with fire and cold; the earthquakes come when he kicks the earth.

alternate_names: Grandmother of Day, Grandmother of Light
primary_sources: Popol Vuh (K'iche' Maya, written c. 1550s; Ximénez manuscript c. 1701)
deities.summary: The divine grandmother, diviner and midwife of creation, who with Xpiyacoc counted the days and who ground the white and yellow maize nine times to make the flesh of the first true humans.

primary_sources: Fray Juan de Córdova, Vocabulario en lengua zapoteca (1578)
Zapotec urn and tomb imagery (Monte Albán)
deities.summary: The uncreated creator of the Zapotecs, without beginning or end, from whom all the pitao (gods) proceed.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE colonial records; Monte Albán imagery
primary_sources: Fray Juan de Córdova, Vocabulario en lengua zapoteca (1578)
Zapotec urn and tomb imagery (Monte Albán)
deities.summary: Lord of death and the underworld, ruling the dead with his consort Xonaxi Quecuya.

primary_sources: Fray Gregorio García, Origen de los indios del Nuevo Mundo (1607)
deities.summary: The primordial creator couple of the Mixtecs, who raised a palace on a mountain above the primeval waters at Apoala and engendered the gods and the first lineages.
The wind god and plumed serpent of the Mixtecs, born from a flint knife, who descended from heaven bearing the sky on his shoulders, gave the Mixtec lords their rule and brought the arts of offering.

primary_sources: Fray Francisco de Alvarado, Vocabulario en lengua mixteca (1593)
deities.summary: The rain god, patron of the Mixtec people, who call themselves Ñuu Savi, "People of the Rain."
The fire and sun god, patron of the Uacúsecha ruling lineage of the Tarascan state, fed by great bonfires that were kept burning on his temples and by the war captives taken in his name.
Moon goddess of fertility and the crops, honored on the island of Jarácuaro, joined to Curicaueri in the alliance of the lake peoples.
The creator mother of the Tarascans, who sends the rain and the clouds and gave birth to the gods; captives were sacrificed to her at Zinapécuaro.

primary_sources: Guaman Poma de Ayala, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (c. 1615)
Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)
Juan de Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas (1551)
deities.summary: The thunder god of the Inca, a man of the sky in shining garments with a sling and a club. The crack of his sling is thunder, its flash lightning, its stone the thunderbolt; he draws water from the Milky Way and pours it as rain. Those struck by lightning and twins were his.

primary_sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)
Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)
deities.summary: Mother Sea and of all waters, from which lakes and springs come; worshipped especially by fishermen of the coast, and mother of the Inca line in some accounts.

primary_sources: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)
José de Acosta, Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590)
deities.summary: The mother of maize, honored in specially shaped ears and dressed maize figures kept for a year to ensure the harvest.
The lords of the mountains, powerful spirits of the high peaks who watch over herds, villages and the weather; offerings of coca and the despacho are made to them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Early Intermediate–Late Horizon (shrine c. 200 CE onward)
primary_sources: Pedro Cieza de León, Crónica del Perú (1553)
deities.summary: The Earth-Maker of the central coast, whose oracle at the great shrine south of Lima was the most famous in the Andes. He made the first people and the food plants, defeated the older god Con, and causes earthquakes when he moves.

primary_sources: Francisco López de Gómara, Historia general de las Indias (1552)
Agustín de Zárate, Historia del descubrimiento y conquista del Perú (1555)
deities.summary: The boneless creator who came from the north, raised and lowered the mountains with his word, and made the first people; when they angered him he withheld the rain and made the coast desert, until Pachacamac came and drove him away.

primary_sources: Moche ceramics and the Huaca de la Luna murals
deities.summary: The fanged creator-hero of the Moche, wearing a jaguar headdress and a serpent belt, who battles sea monsters, descends to the underworld and presides over sacrifice.
deities.tradition_claim: The name is taken from colonial Mochica vocabulary and applied to the Moche fanged figure by modern interpreters.

deities.summary: The snow-mountain god of Huarochirí, born from five eggs as five falcons that became five men, who defeated the fire-god Huallallo Carhuincho with rain and floods and established the order of the Yauyos people.

The wandering trickster-creator of Huarochirí, who walked as a ragged beggar, made the terraces and canals with his word, fathered a child on Cavillaca through a fruit, and pursued her to the sea; he gave and took animals their traits.

primary_sources: Juan de Castellanos, Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias (1589)
Lucas Fernández de Piedrahita, Historia general (1688)
deities.summary: The bearded civilizer who came from the east, taught the Muisca weaving, agriculture, law and morality, and when the goddess Chía (or Chibchacum) flooded the savanna, struck the rocks with his staff to open the Tequendama Falls and drain the waters.

primary_sources: Juan de Castellanos, Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias (1589)
Lucas Fernández de Piedrahita, Historia general (1688)
deities.summary: The moon goddess, beautiful and rebellious, who taught pleasure and dance against Bochica's rules and flooded the savanna; Bochica turned her into the moon (or an owl).
deities.tradition_claim: Chroniclers sometimes merge Chía and Huitaca, sometimes distinguish them.

primary_sources: Juan de Castellanos, Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias (1589)
Lucas Fernández de Piedrahita, Historia general (1688)
deities.summary: Patron of farmers and merchants who, angered by the people, flooded the savanna; Bochica punished him by making him bear the earth on his shoulders, so earthquakes come when he shifts the load.

primary_sources: Juan de Castellanos, Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias (1589)
Lucas Fernández de Piedrahita, Historia general (1688)
deities.summary: The sun god, husband of Chía, to whom the temple of Sogamoso was dedicated and to whom the Muisca made offerings of gold.
Malignant spirits and forces of disorder that cause sickness, misfortune and death, sent by kalku (sorcerers); the machi fights them in the healing rite.
The serpent of the waters who raised the sea to flood the world and drown the people.
The serpent of the earth and mountains who raised the land higher and higher as Kai Kai Vilu raised the sea, saving the people who climbed onto him.

The True Father Ñamandu, First One, who unfolded himself from the primal darkness, made the foundation of human speech (ayvu rapyta) and the flame and mist of being, and then created the other divine fathers and the earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Tupi-Guarani usage recorded 16th c. CE
primary_sources: Jesuit grammars (José de Anchieta, Arte de gramática, 1595)
deities.summary: The divine father of thunder and rain in the west, one of the four great fathers created by Ñamandu; his voice is thunder and he sends the rains.
deities.tradition_claim: Jesuit missionaries adopted "Tupã" to name the Christian God in Tupi and Guarani.

deities.summary: The sun, elder twin brother of Jasy (moon), culture hero who avenged his mother killed by the jaguars and established the order of the world before ascending to the sky.
The moon, younger twin of Kuaray, mischievous and clumsy, whose blunders the sun repairs; he governs the night and the women's cycle.

The culture hero and lawgiver of the Vaupés peoples, born of a virgin, who gave men the sacred flutes and the secret laws of initiation; he was burned and from his ashes grew the palm whose wood makes the flutes. Women may not see the flutes.
deities.tradition_claim: Jesuit missionaries used "Jurupari" for the Devil, a reading the Vaupés peoples do not share.

primary_sources: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
iconography: zemí with arms spiraling in opposite directions
deities.summary: The furious zemí of the hurricane, Lady of the Winds, who sends her herald Guataubá with thunder and Coatrisquie with floods, and destroys whatever stands in her path.

primary_sources: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
deities.summary: Lord of Coaybay, the land of the dead, where the opía (spirits of the dead) live; they hide by day and come out at night to eat guava and walk among the living, recognizable because they have no navel.

primary_sources: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
deities.summary: The dog-shaped zemí who guarded the dead and at night ran off into the forest; when the Spanish came he escaped into a lagoon and was never seen again.

primary_sources: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
deities.summary: Eldest of four twin brothers born of one mother, culture hero who stole cassava bread and cohoba from the old man Bayamanaco; spat on, his back swelled and from it came the turtle, the first woman, who bore their children.

primary_sources: Iñupiat and Bering Strait oral tradition
deities.summary: Raven the creator of the Iñupiat and Bering Strait peoples, who woke in darkness, made the land and the first man from a pea-pod, and brought light to the world.

primary_sources: Knud Rasmussen, Report of the Fifth Thule Expedition 1921–24 (ethnographic collection)
Hans Egede, Det gamle Grønlands nye Perlustration (1741)
deities.summary: The great helping spirit of the Greenlandic angakkuit, chief of the tornait, from whom shamans receive their power and with whom they consult on journeys to the sea-mother and the sky.
deities.tradition_claim: Danish missionaries in Greenland identified Tornarsuk with the Devil, an equation the angakkuit did not make.

primary_sources: Knud Rasmussen, Report of the Fifth Thule Expedition 1921–24 (ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: The moon man, who pursued his sister Malina (the sun) after a forbidden encounter in the dark; he chases her endlessly across the sky, forgets to eat and wastes away, then disappears to hunt and returns.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; carved crests 18th–19th c. CE
primary_sources: Northwest Coast oral tradition and crest histories
deities.summary: The great bird whose wingbeats are thunder and whose eyes flash lightning, who seizes whales from the sea and battles the lightning serpent; ancestor of noble lineages who display him on their poles.

primary_sources: Lakota narratives recorded by James R. Walker (Lakota Belief and Ritual, ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: Rock, the first of all beings, who existed in the darkness and was soft and full of power. To create, he poured out his blood (the blue waters) and spread himself into the earth Maka and the sky, until he became hard and powerless.

primary_sources: Lakota narratives recorded by James R. Walker (ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: Sky, the supreme judge and source of force and motion, who sits above the other powers, gives spirit to living things and judges gods and humans.

The All Spirit who existed alone in the void; he made the great water and the water-birds, and when the little coot brought mud from the bottom he placed it on Grandmother Turtle's back, and it grew into the earth.

The prophet and culture hero who went into the sacred mountain (Bear Butte) and brought back the four Sacred Arrows (Maahotse), the laws of the Council of Forty-Four, and prophecies of the coming of strangers.
The Master of Breath, who gives and takes life; he is honored at the Green Corn ceremony, when the sacred fire is rekindled and the people are renewed.
Rabbit the trickster of the Muscogee, who stole fire for the people and fools the stronger animals with his wits.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; rock paintings (Agawa Rock) pre-contact
iconography: horned lynx with spined back and long tail (Agawa Rock)
deities.summary: The Great Lynx, the horned underwater panther of the lakes, who owns the copper and stirs storms and rapids; enemy of the Thunderbirds.
The Thunderbirds who bring the spring rains and war against the underwater powers; they come from the west and are grandfathers to the people.

primary_sources: Silas Rand, Legends of the Micmacs (1894) (ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: The great transformer and culture hero of the Wabanaki, who shaped the land, named the animals, reduced the dangerous giant beasts to their present size, defeated the water-hoarding monster, and will return when the people need him.
Glooscap's wolf-twin, who made the troublesome things — rough land, poisonous creatures — and plotted his brother's death until Glooscap destroyed him.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art c. 750 CE onward; Hopi katsina tradition
deities.summary: The humpbacked flute player, bringer of fertility, rain and seeds, whose music warms the earth and whose hump carries seeds or gifts.
The god of germination who lives in the underworld and sends up the sprouting seeds; brother or husband of the corn mother.

alternate_names: Holder of the Roads of Life
deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
primary_sources: Zuni oral tradition (recorded by Frank Hamilton Cushing, Outlines of Zuñi Creation Myths, 1896)
deities.summary: The All-Container, the He-She who alone existed in the void; by thinking outward he/she made mists and from his own substance became the Sun Father, whose light formed the Earth Mother and Sky Father.
deities.tradition_claim: Some later Zuni and scholarly accounts read the name as a collective term for the life-giving powers rather than one god.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
iconography: carved wooden war-god images on mesa shrines
deities.summary: The twin war gods, sons of the Sun Father, who led the people up from the underworld, slew the monsters that preyed on them, and protect the Zuni; their images stand in shrines on the mesas.
The great plumed and horned water serpent who lives in springs and the underworld waters; when offended he floods the land.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th–20th c. CE
deities.summary: Thought Woman, who thinks things into being: by her thought the world, the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti, and all things came forth; she guided the sisters from the underworld and taught them to pray and plant.
Corn Mother, first mother of the Keres people, who emerged from the underworld with her sister and planted the seeds Thought Woman gave; she returned below to Shipap, where the dead go back to her.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The Holy Person who helped the Hero Twins on their way to their father the Sun and gave them the life-feathers that protected them; she taught the Diné women to weave on the loom her husband Spider Man built.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
deities.summary: Formed from the white and yellow corn ears in the lower worlds, First Man built the first hogan, placed the stars with First Woman, and holds the medicine bundle of creation; both creator and source of witchcraft.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
deities.summary: Formed with First Man from corn in the lower worlds; with him she ordered the world. After the separation of the sexes and its disasters, the monsters were born of the women's transgressions.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The Sun Bearer, who carries the sun across the sky; father of the Hero Twins by Changing Woman, who tested them severely before arming them with lightning to slay the monsters.
The first woman, who survived the flood in an abalone shell, bore Child of Water to the rain and the sun, and protected him from the monster; every Apache girl becomes her in the Sunrise Ceremony.
Son of White Painted Woman and the rain, the monster-slayer who killed the giant Owl-Man and the other monsters that ate the people.
Elder brother of Child of Water (or Child of Water himself in some groups), culture hero and slayer of monsters, who chose the ways of the hunting and the horse.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; founding variously dated c. 1142–1450 CE
primary_sources: Kaianere'kó:wa (Great Law of Peace, oral recitation)
deities.summary: The messenger born of a virgin among the Wendat, who crossed the lake in a white stone canoe, combed the snakes from the hair of the tyrant Tadodaho with Hiawatha, and planted the Tree of Great Peace uniting the Five Nations under the Great Law.

primary_sources: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900) (ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: The great horned serpent with a blazing crystal on its forehead and rings of color along its body; to see it is death, but the crystal (ulunsuti) taken from it gives the shaman the power of prophecy.

primary_sources: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900) (ethnographic collection)
deities.summary: The sons of Kanati and Selu — the good son and the Wild Boy born from the blood of game — who released the animals, killed their mother and caused her to give the corn, and became the thunder in the west.

primary_sources: Nez Perce and Sahaptin oral tradition
deities.summary: Coyote the transformer of the Plateau, who killed the monster in the Kamiah valley and made the peoples from its body, broke the fish dams so salmon could swim upriver, and readied the world for the human beings who were coming.

The creator who came down on a rope of feathers to Turtle floating on the primal waters, made the earth from the mud Turtle brought up and created the first people; Coyote opposed his plan and brought death.
Coyote who argued with Earth Initiate that people must die so the world would not be crowded, and whose own son was the first to die.

facets.facet_name: Owner of the sacred leaves
facets.core_claim: Osanyin alone knows the secret virtue of every leaf; the other orisha received their portions of herbal power only when Shango's wife Oya scattered his calabash with the wind.

facets.facet_name: Hunter whose arrow never misses
facets.core_claim: Ochosi fires one arrow and it always finds its target; he hunts the prey that feeds the community and pursues the wrongdoer so that justice is done.

facets.facet_name: The ancestors who return in masquerade
facets.core_claim: The dead do not vanish; the Egungun come back through the masked dancer, whose body no one may touch, to judge, bless and protect the lineage.

facets.facet_name: Owner of the abyssal sea
facets.core_claim: Olokun rules the bottom of the ocean where no light reaches; all the wealth of the sea is Olokun's, and Olokun's anger is the flood.

facets.facet_name: The sacred twins
facets.core_claim: Twins are a single soul in two bodies and bring wealth and blessing to those who honor them; the carved ere ibeji keeps a dead twin in the family.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the farm and harvest
facets.core_claim: Orisha Oko makes the soil yield; his iron staff and his yams are the wealth of the farmer.

facets.facet_name: The one who spread the first earth at Ife
facets.core_claim: When Obatala was overcome by palm wine, Oduduwa took the bag of earth, poured it on the waters at Ife, and the hen scratched it out into the land.

facets.facet_name: First king and father of the Yoruba dynasties
facets.core_claim: Oduduwa is the first Ooni of Ife; every legitimate crown descends from him.

facets.facet_name: Personal deity of destiny
facets.core_claim: Before birth each soul kneels and chooses its Ori in heaven; the head one carries is the god one carries, and it is propitiated before all others.

facets.facet_name: Death, warrior of the ajogun
facets.core_claim: Iku is the chief of the ajogun who wage war on human life; he cannot be destroyed, only appeased and delayed through the sacrifices Ifá prescribes.

facets.facet_name: Earth-lord of smallpox and healing
facets.core_claim: Sakpata owns the earth; its grains erupt on the skin as smallpox when he is offended and he withdraws them when he is appeased.

facets.facet_name: Thunderer who punishes wrongdoing
facets.core_claim: Xevioso hurls thunderstones at those who lie and steal and sends the rain that makes the fields fertile.

facets.facet_name: Iron, the tool of creation
facets.core_claim: Gu is the cutting tool of Mawu-Lisa; with him the earth was made habitable and humanity received the arts of iron.

facets.facet_name: Serpent who carries and encircles the world
facets.core_claim: Aido-Hwedo bore the creator in his mouth and now lies coiled beneath the earth, tail in mouth, so it does not sink into the sea; if he ate his tail the world would end.

facets.facet_name: Master of the sea
facets.core_claim: Agbe rules the ocean and the vodun of the waters; offerings are given to him on the shore.

facets.facet_name: The written destiny revealed by divination
facets.core_claim: Mawu wrote each person's destiny; Fa is that writing, and through the palm nuts the diviner reads it so people can live in accord with it.

facets.facet_name: River god of war and thunder
facets.core_claim: Tano is the strongest of Nyame's sons, given the river and its people; he fights for them and judges their wrongdoing.

facets.facet_name: Elder son tricked of his inheritance
facets.core_claim: Nyame meant to give Bia the fertile land, but the goat told Tano to go first; Bia received the barren country instead.

facets.facet_name: Forest monster and ally of witches
facets.core_claim: Sasabonsam lies in wait in the tall trees and catches with his hooked feet those who walk the forest alone.

facets.facet_name: Trickster of war and chaos
facets.core_claim: Ekwensu stirs violence and cunning; warriors invoke his frenzy, and the wise keep him at a distance once the fight is over.
facets.scholarly_note: Christian missionaries chose Ekwensu to translate "Devil" in the Igbo Bible, a move many Igbo traditionalists reject as a mistranslation of an ambivalent trickster.

facets.facet_name: God of the strong right hand
facets.core_claim: Ikenga is the power of a man's own right hand to succeed; through it he acts in the world and his Chi works.

facets.facet_name: Spirit who calls the diviner
facets.core_claim: Agwu gives the dibia sight and medicine; to the one who resists his call he sends confusion and illness.

facets.facet_name: The sun, eye of Chukwu
facets.core_claim: Anyanwu sees everything under heaven and lights the path of those who live rightly.

facets.facet_name: Personal destiny-spirit
facets.core_claim: Each person's chi is a spark of Chukwu that chose their destiny with them; no one rises beyond the will of their chi.

facets.facet_name: High creator God
facets.core_claim: Osanobua made all things and stands above the gods; his children rule the realms of water, earth and death on his behalf.

facets.facet_name: King of the waters, giver of wealth and children
facets.core_claim: Olokun rules a palace beneath the waters as the Oba rules on land; he sends children, riches and health to those who keep his altars.

facets.facet_name: King of death
facets.core_claim: Ogiuwu owns death; all who die enter his realm, and his shrine is fed with blood.

facets.facet_name: God of the shining mountain
facets.core_claim: Ngai made all things and dwells on Kirinyaga; he gave the land to Gikuyu and is approached under the sacred fig.

facets.facet_name: First parents of the Kikuyu clans
facets.core_claim: Ngai showed Gikuyu the land from the mountain top and gave him Mumbi; from their daughters come all the clans.

facets.facet_name: Divinity who withdrew to the sky
facets.core_claim: Nhialic created all and once walked near people; after the first woman's hoe struck the sky he went far off, and now is reached through prayer and sacrifice.

facets.facet_name: Free-divinity of rain and lightning
facets.core_claim: Deng sends the rain and strikes with lightning; his name is the word for rain.

facets.facet_name: First woman and gardener
facets.core_claim: Abuk wanted more than the one grain a day Nhialic allowed; she pounded more, her pestle struck the sky, and he withdrew.

facets.facet_name: First man and power of the sun
facets.core_claim: Garang was made with Abuk and remains a power who seizes people with fevers and must be honored.

facets.facet_name: Spirit of the sky, everywhere like wind
facets.core_claim: Kwoth is like the wind, invisible yet everywhere; all things come from him and the lesser spirits are his refractions.

facets.facet_name: Supreme God above all spirits
facets.core_claim: Nzambi a Mpungu made the world and all its powers; he is beyond images, and all lesser force flows from him.

facets.facet_name: Spirit bound in a sacred object
facets.core_claim: A nkisi is a dead spirit made to work through medicines in a figure; each nail driven into the nkondi wakes it to enforce an oath or punish a wrong.

facets.facet_name: The water-boundary between living and dead
facets.core_claim: Kalunga is the shining water between the two worlds; to die is to go under it and to be born is to come back across it, as the sun does each day.

facets.facet_name: Spirits of springs, pools and rocks
facets.core_claim: The bisimbi inhabit sacred waters and stones; they guard the community whose land they live in and punish those who violate their places.

facets.facet_name: The rainbow tyrant
facets.core_claim: Nkongolo ate in public, married his sisters and ruled by force; he is the uncivilized kingship that true Luba royalty replaced.

facets.facet_name: Hunter who brought refined kingship
facets.core_claim: Mbidi Kiluwe hid when he ate and drank, revealing a dignity unknown to Nkongolo; from him comes the sacred blood of Luba kings.

facets.facet_name: Founder of sacred Luba kingship
facets.core_claim: Kalala Ilunga escaped Nkongolo's trap, returned with an army, and beheaded the rainbow king; his descendants are the bulopwe, the sacred rulers.

facets.facet_name: High God of rain who speaks from the caves
facets.core_claim: Mwari created people and sends the rain; his voice answers petitioners from the shrine caves, and the land prospers when he is honored.

facets.facet_name: Royal ancestral spirit and guardian of the land
facets.core_claim: Nehanda is a guardian of the whole land; she possesses her mediums to guide the people and defend the soil of the ancestors.

facets.facet_name: Prophet-guardian spirit
facets.core_claim: Chaminuka sees what is to come and speaks through his medium to warn and protect the people.

facets.facet_name: The one who appeared first
facets.core_claim: uMvelinqangi was before everything; thunder is his voice and he is greater than every ancestor.

facets.facet_name: Heavenly princess of rain and crops
facets.core_claim: Nomkhubulwana walks the fields veiled in mist; where she is honored by the young women the maize grows and the rain falls.

facets.facet_name: Ancestors of the lineage
facets.core_claim: The amadlozi live on and care for their homestead; neglect angers them, and honoring them brings health and luck.

facets.facet_name: Witch-sent malicious sprite
facets.core_claim: The tokoloshe is a familiar that the umthakathi (witch) sends to bite, frighten and sicken; the inyanga's medicine drives it away.

facets.facet_name: Creator of the defended world
facets.core_claim: Qamata made the earth and defended it from the dragon of the sea; travelers honor him by adding a stone to the roadside cairn.

facets.facet_name: Creator in the eastern sky
facets.core_claim: ǂGao!na made all things and sends rain and game; the stories of his foolish early deeds are told alongside prayers to him.

facets.facet_name: Trickster who shoots arrows of death
facets.core_claim: ǁGauwa and the dead shoot the small arrows that bring misfortune; the healers in trance draw them out and argue the dead away.

facets.facet_name: Rain-giving god of the red dawn
facets.core_claim: Tsui-ǁGoab gives rain and life; he battled ǁGaunab many times, was wounded in the knee, died and rose again, and finally triumphed.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the dark sky and death
facets.core_claim: ǁGaunab wars against the rain-giver and kills people; though defeated and thrown down, he still lurks in the dark to strike.

facets.facet_name: Hero of the many graves
facets.core_claim: Heitsi-eibib defeated the monster Ga-gorib and died and returned again and again; every cairn is one of his graves.

facets.facet_name: Reborn serpent-ancestor of the earth
facets.core_claim: Lébé was buried and returned as a snake; each night he licks the Hogon to give him the strength of the earth for the people.

facets.facet_name: River spirit who ordered the world
facets.core_claim: Faro descended as water and rain, restored the order Pemba had broken, and gave people speech, the calendar and the rules of life.

facets.facet_name: First creator who overreached
facets.core_claim: Pemba shaped the earth and the first woman, Musokoroni; he made himself a tree to be worshipped and claimed creation as his own.

facets.facet_name: First woman of disorder
facets.core_claim: Musokoroni refused Pemba and wandered the earth in frenzy; wherever she went she sowed both disorder and the first crops.

facets.facet_name: Supreme God of the Serer
facets.core_claim: Roog is the source of everything and is approached through the pangool ancestors; the saltigue read his will for the coming season.

facets.facet_name: Ancestral intercessor spirits
facets.core_claim: The pangool carry prayers to Roog and protect the families and lands that keep their shrines.

facets.facet_name: Creator and father of the gods
facets.core_claim: Katonda created the world and everything in it; the lubaale serve under him.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the lake and of plenty
facets.core_claim: Mukasa calms the lake, sends the fish and grants children; he asks no blood, only offerings of cattle and beer.

facets.facet_name: War god of Buganda
facets.core_claim: Kibuka flew above the battle in a cloud and shot the enemy with arrows; Buganda won while he was at its side.

facets.facet_name: Death who followed the first couple
facets.core_claim: Gulu warned Kintu and Nambi not to turn back; Nambi did, and Walumbe came with them. His brother Kayikuuzi chased him but he hid in the ground.

facets.facet_name: First man and founding king
facets.core_claim: Kintu came with one cow and won Nambi by completing the impossible tasks Gulu set; the kings of Buganda descend from him.

facets.facet_name: Mother of fertility
facets.core_claim: Ateetee is the women's protector; married women gather to sing to her and she grants children and safety in birth.

facets.facet_name: Creator who gives the breath of life
facets.core_claim: Zanahary made all and gives the breath; prayers begin with him before the ancestors.

facets.facet_name: The ancestors of the famadihana
facets.core_claim: The razana watch over their descendants and are owed tombs, offerings and the periodic rewrapping of their bones.

facets.facet_name: Lion god of war and royal victory
facets.core_claim: Apedemak, splendid god, lion of the south, gives the king victory over his enemies and feeds the land; Meroitic kings built temples to him as their own god.

facets.facet_name: Ram-headed Amun who chooses the kings
facets.core_claim: Amun of Napata dwells inside the holy mountain; he names the king by oracle, and the king rules as his son.

facets.facet_name: God of procreation and doorway guardian
facets.core_claim: Sebiumeker is the begetter, standing at the gate of the temple to guard what lies within.

facets.facet_name: The good companion and hunter-guardian
facets.core_claim: Arensnuphis accompanies and protects; he hunts and brings back the far-wandering goddess.

facets.facet_name: Ram-horned oracle god of the desert
facets.core_claim: Ammon speaks from his oasis sanctuary to all who make the desert crossing; kings seek his word and his sonship.

facets.facet_name: Bull god carried into battle
facets.core_claim: Gurzil, son of Ammon, goes before the tribe in battle in his bull image and gives his people courage.

facets.facet_name: Rain god who seeks his bride
facets.core_claim: Anzar dried up the springs until the girl he loved came to him; when they joined, the rain returned, and the rite of the Bride of Anzar renews that union.

facets.facet_name: Patroness against lightning and sudden death
facets.core_claim: Saint Barbara intercedes for those in danger from lightning, fire and explosion, for God avenged her with the thunderbolt.

facets.facet_name: Patron of lepers and the sick
facets.core_claim: Saint Lazarus, who suffered sores in this life and was comforted in the next, intercedes for the sick and the outcast.

facets.facet_name: Patroness of the harbor and seafarers
facets.core_claim: Our Lady of Regla watches over the harbor and all who travel by sea.

facets.facet_name: Keeper of the keys of heaven
facets.core_claim: To Peter were given the keys: what he binds on earth is bound in heaven, and he opens the gate to the blessed.

facets.facet_name: Warrior saint who slew the dragon
facets.core_claim: Saint George, armored for Christ, overcomes the dragon and defends the weak; soldiers call on him in battle.

facets.facet_name: Finder of lost things and patron of travelers
facets.core_claim: Saint Anthony restores what is lost and opens the way for the traveler and the poor.

facets.facet_name: Child pilgrim who aids prisoners and travelers
facets.core_claim: The Holy Child goes out by night with his basket and staff to feed prisoners and guide travelers; his worn shoes are the sign of his journeys.

facets.facet_name: Scarred Black Madonna, protectress of her people
facets.core_claim: Our Lady of Częstochowa, wounded in her image, defends her people and is crowned their Queen.

facets.facet_name: Patroness of Cuba who came on the waters
facets.core_claim: Our Lady of Charity calmed the sea for the three Juans and remains the mother of all Cubans.

facets.facet_name: Ransomer of captives
facets.core_claim: Our Lady of Mercy frees the captive; her white mantle shelters all who are bound.

facets.facet_name: Virgin of the candle and the purification
facets.core_claim: Our Lady of Candelaria carries the light of Christ presented in the Temple.

facets.facet_name: Warrior apostle on the white horse
facets.core_claim: Santiago rides into battle for the faithful; Christ named him a son of thunder.

facets.facet_name: Forerunner and baptizer
facets.core_claim: John prepares the way and baptizes with water for repentance.

facets.facet_name: Bishop who drove out the serpents
facets.core_claim: Saint Patrick, with his staff, banished the serpents from Ireland and planted the faith.

facets.facet_name: Patron of farmers
facets.core_claim: Saint Isidore prays and the angels plow; he blesses the fields and the farmer's labor.

facets.facet_name: Martyr pierced by arrows
facets.core_claim: Saint Sebastian, pierced by arrows and not slain, protects the city and those struck by plague.

facets.facet_name: Mother whose heart is pierced by sorrow
facets.core_claim: Mary's heart is pierced by seven swords; her sorrow joins Christ's suffering and comforts all who grieve.

facets.facet_name: Mystic of poverty and creation
facets.core_claim: Francis, poor for Christ, bears his wounds and preaches to all creatures.

facets.facet_name: Twin physician-martyrs
facets.core_claim: The holy twins heal freely and protect children.

facets.facet_name: The sinless Virgin standing on the serpent
facets.core_claim: Mary, conceived without stain, crushes the serpent and stands upon the moon.

facets.facet_name: The Good God beyond the lwa
facets.core_claim: Bondye made everything and governs it, but he is too great to be served directly; the lwa carry his will and our prayers.

facets.facet_name: Spirits of death and sacred humor
facets.core_claim: The Gede are the dead who laugh; they guard the cemetery, mock the pretensions of the living, protect children and decide whether the sick will die.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the dead and guardian of graves
facets.core_claim: Maman Brigitte protects tombs marked with crosses and renders harsh justice; she is invoked against curses and for healing those near death.

facets.facet_name: The sacred twins
facets.core_claim: The Marasa are the first dead and the first born; they are stronger than the great lwa and are fed before them.

facets.facet_name: Scarred warrior-mother of the Petwo rite
facets.core_claim: Dantor will knife anyone who harms her children; she stood with the rebels at Bois Caïman and protects single mothers and abused women.

facets.facet_name: First priest and lord of the sacred tree
facets.core_claim: Loko is the master of initiation; he consecrates priests and judges their work, and lives in the great trees of the peristil.

facets.facet_name: Master of the night crossroads
facets.core_claim: Kalfou opens the way to the powers of the night; what Legba opens by day, Kalfou opens by dark, for good or ill.

facets.facet_name: Peasant lwa of the harvest
facets.core_claim: Kouzen Zaka works the land and blesses the harvest; he loves his crops and drives a hard bargain.

facets.facet_name: Rainbow serpent, consort of Damballa
facets.core_claim: Ayida-Wedo arches across the heavens as the rainbow; with Damballa she joins sky and earth and the waters.

facets.facet_name: God who governs the world directly
facets.core_claim: Olofi withdrew from the world after creation, but it is still Olofi who gave each orisha its ashé and who receives the final word in Ifá.

facets.facet_name: Owner of roads who opens and closes the way
facets.core_claim: Elegguá stands behind the door of every house; he opens the way for those who feed him and closes it for those who forget him.

facets.facet_name: Mother of life and queen of the sea
facets.core_claim: Yemayá is the ocean from which all life comes; she nurses the world and her anger is the storm at sea.

facets.facet_name: Lord of epidemic and healing
facets.core_claim: Babalú-Ayé sends and lifts disease; the suffering one who knows suffering is the one who heals it.

facets.facet_name: Warrior of iron and labor
facets.core_claim: Ogún labors without rest; his iron opens the forest and his anger brings accidents with metal.

facets.facet_name: Orisha of river, love and sweetness
facets.core_claim: Ochún brings love, children and wealth; she won over Ogún with honey when no warrior could bring him out of the forest.

facets.facet_name: Owner of the winds and the cemetery gate
facets.core_claim: Oyá guards the cemetery gates and sweeps away the old with her whirlwind; she fights at Changó's side with lightning.

facets.facet_name: Messenger who moves the axé
facets.core_claim: Exu is fed first because without him nothing moves; he carries words and offerings between the worlds.

facets.facet_name: Warrior orixá of iron
facets.core_claim: Ogum is the warrior who opens the way; his tools make agriculture and civilization possible.

facets.facet_name: Hunter-king of Ketu
facets.core_claim: Oxóssi, king of Ketu, never misses; his one arrow brings abundance to the people.

facets.facet_name: Straw-covered lord of disease and cure
facets.core_claim: Omolu hides under his straw; he brings and removes pestilence, and in the Olubajé feast he receives popcorn to heal the community.

facets.facet_name: Mistress of wind and the dead
facets.core_claim: Iansã commands the eguns with her whisk and rides the storm; she is the only orixá who does not fear the dead.

facets.facet_name: King of thunder and justice
facets.core_claim: Xangô judges with fire; his oxê falls on liars, and he protects the just.

facets.facet_name: Supreme God of Umbanda
facets.core_claim: Zambi created the universe and rules it through the orixás and the phalanxes of spirits who work for charity.

facets.facet_name: Spirits of enslaved elders turned healers
facets.core_claim: The pretos velhos suffered and forgave; their humility makes them strong to heal, pray and give counsel.

facets.facet_name: Indigenous spirit healers of the forest
facets.core_claim: The caboclos know every herb of the forest; they arrive with a cry and cleanse and heal those who come to the terreiro.

facets.facet_name: Guardians of the crossroads and the street
facets.core_claim: Exus guard the gate of the terreiro and do the hard work in the dark places; they serve the law of karma and the orders of the orixás.

facets.facet_name: Queen of the street and of desire
facets.core_claim: Pombagira knows the heart and the body; she opens roads in love and defends women, and demands respect and her offerings of champagne and roses.

facets.facet_name: Lord who locks and opens the roads
facets.core_claim: Tranca-Ruas closes the roads against enemies and opens them for those who serve him; nothing passes the crossroads without his leave.

facets.facet_name: Queen of the pombagiras
facets.core_claim: Maria Padilha commands the hearts of lovers and the fortunes of women; her workings are powerful and her price must be paid.

facets.facet_name: Supreme God of the Congo rules
facets.core_claim: Nsambi is above and below; from him come the powers that the palero works through the nganga.

facets.facet_name: Mpungu of iron and war
facets.core_claim: Zarabanda is iron that cuts and binds; he works hard and fights hard for those who feed him.

facets.facet_name: Mpungu of the seven lightning bolts
facets.core_claim: Siete Rayos throws his lightning at enemies and burns away obstacles.

facets.facet_name: Star who guards the roads
facets.core_claim: Lucero lights the way at the crossing of the roads; he must be greeted before any work begins.

facets.facet_name: Mistress of the cemetery wind
facets.core_claim: Centella rules the cemetery and the whirlwind; she commands the dead in the nganga.

facets.facet_name: Supreme creator of Winti
facets.core_claim: Anana made all things and gave the winti their domains; he is too high to receive offerings himself.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the earth pantheon
facets.core_claim: Mama Aisa owns the ground; the first drink is poured to her and she protects the land and its people.

facets.facet_name: The great snake spirit
facets.core_claim: Papa is the serpent who knows the secrets of the earth; his mediums heal and prophesy.

facets.facet_name: Supreme sky god of Kumina
facets.core_claim: King Zombi is the highest power, above the ancestors and spirits who come in the dance.

facets.facet_name: Patron orisha of the Trinidad faith
facets.core_claim: Shango leads the powers in Trinidad; his thunder protects the faithful and punishes the wicked.

facets.facet_name: Warrior orisha of iron
facets.core_claim: Ogun stands guard with his sword and fights for the faithful.

facets.facet_name: Wise-woman spirit guide
facets.core_claim: La Madama brings her herbs, her cigar and her prayers to cleanse and protect those in her care.

facets.facet_name: Indigenous warrior spirit guide
facets.core_claim: El Indio stands in the medium's spiritual court as protector and fights the intranquil spirits away.

facets.facet_name: Unbroken trickster-hero of the enslaved
facets.core_claim: High John came over walking on the waves of sound; he outwitted the master every time and left his spirit in the root, so that those who carry it cannot be beaten.

facets.facet_name: Initiator at the midnight crossroads
facets.core_claim: Go to the crossroads at midnight; the big black man will come, take your instrument and play it, and give you mastery of it.

facets.facet_name: She of the Jade Skirt, lady of flowing waters
facets.core_claim: Chalchiuhtlicue rules rivers, lakes and springs and the waters of birth; she presided over the fourth Sun, which ended in flood.

facets.facet_name: Eater of filth, purifier of sin
facets.core_claim: Tlazolteotl inspires lust and transgression and then devours the filth of sin when it is confessed before her priests, making the sinner clean.

facets.facet_name: Cloud Serpent, the hunter of the Milky Way
facets.core_claim: Mixcoatl is the hunter whose body is the Milky Way; he first drew fire with the drill and is father of the Mimixcoa.

facets.facet_name: The Maize God
